subject: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan

messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
parts:
Hi folks -

Another modeling question for the list.

I'm working on a model with a single binary exposure (A) a binary diagnostic measure (B) and a binary disease outcome (C). I want to know how much of the effect of A  on C, i.e. the exposure on the development of disease, is detected by the diagnostic test, and how much goes under the radar, i.e. isn't picked up by the diagnostic test, so essentially just the A -> C relationship. 

I know a priori that the A -> C relationship is weaker than the  A -> B -> C relationship, i.e. the diagnostic test is a pretty good predictor of disease. Individuals may also have a positive B in the absence of A (i.e they were infected before exposure to B), but those with B not caused by A should be much less likely to develop disease. But this means that A could cause C conceivably without causing B.

I have two ideas about how to model this relationship, one of which I've tried, the other I'm considering:

1) Model the impact of A -> C via B by treating positive results for B among those exposed to A as a mixture of A and non-A causes. So Pr(C | A = 1, B = 1) = rho*Pr(C |A -> B ) + (1-rho)*Pr(C | all other B), where rho is the proportion of B attributable to A when A = 1, where the coefficient for positive values of B resulting from A is represented by A -> B, and the effect of positive B not caused by A is represented by 'all other B'.

The problem with this approach is that it has a lot of moving parts and involves a not terribly well-identified latent variable for A -> B. As a result, when I adjust for the A -> C relationship, the coefficient for C | A -> B blows up and the A -> C shrinks towards zero or becomes negative, even though the C | A -> B relationship is pretty stable in the absence of a covariate for A->C. But this isn't particularly satisfying since it doesn't allow us to explicitly model the A -> C relationship and necessarily tilts the model in the direction of a stronger A -> B -> C relationship.

2) My alternate idea is to take more of a post-stratification approach, in which I model both levels separately, i.e. include  the A -> C and B -> C relationships in a model for C and then estimate the effect of A -> B in its own model, and then predict the proportion of C due to the effect of A via B (i.e. A->B) using an MRP-like approach. 

I also know that from a predictive perspective, this model should do a better job of replicating the C data than the A -> B -> C model. My only qualms about this approach relate to being unsure of the best way to induce a correlation between the two levels of the model. In the pre-Stan era, I would have approached this using a parametric or nonparametric bootstrap. My gut instinct using Stan is to just to model the fixed effects for the B & C levels using a single multivariate normal, and to allow any random effects for both levels (in this case just intercepts) to also be correlated. This way, if the A -> B and A -> C effects are strongly correlated, this should be reflected in the MRP results. But before going in this direction I wanted to check to see that this actually made sense. 

Apologies if any of the above isn't clear enough; please let me know. 

Any ideas/suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

thanks,
Jon

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
parts:
Let me preface this with "I am not an epidemiologist" :-)
And I didn't understand exactly which pieces of data were
observed and what the population was.

Why not just try to set up the joint model

p(A, B, C) = p(A) * p(C | A) * p(B | C)

so that p(B | C) is the usual diagnostic accuracy model of
sensitivity and specificity? Then you can do any of the
conditional inferences you want.

I wasn't exactly sure what you wanted to compare, but it
felt like

P(C | A, B) vs. P(C | A)

I'd be inclined to measure this kind of thing via mutual information --- that
is, how much B (diagnostic test) measurement be expected to reduce the uncertainty
about C (disease status), conditioned on exposure (and/or non-exposure
if you have non-exposure data).

- Bob

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
parts:
Hi Jon,

It sounds like you're interested in the sensitivity and specificity of test B to pick up a causal link between A and C. However, you also write "the A -> B -> C relationship", suggesting that B is part of the causal chain. Can you clarify please, or describe the context in more detail? As an infectious disease epidemiologist myself, I'm having a hard time grasping what you want to do. I will try to rephrase the problem.

So it's two parameters you are interested in: sensitivity and specificity. From your message, I gather you assume that

  1. sensitivity is <100% as "A could cause C conceivably without causing B", and
  2. specificity is <100% as "individuals may also have a positive B in the absence of A".

Assuming that you observed A and C without measurement error, there are four "outcomes" in the data:

A   C
0   0
0   1
1   0
1   1

 

And you want to know how well B=1 detects (A=1, C=1):

A   C   B
0   0   0   true negative
0   1   0   true negative 
1   0   0   true negative
1   1   0   false negative 
0   0   1   false positive
0   1   1   false positive
1   0   1   false positive
1   1   1   true positive


So this is very straightforward, still assuming that you observed A and C without measurement error:

sensitivity = sum(true.positive) / sum(A=1, C=1)
specificity = sum(true.negative) / (N - (sum(A=1, C=1))


Assuming beta-priors for sensitivity and specificity, you can formulate analytical solutions for their marginal posteriors.

When you want to account for measurement error in A and C, you will need to model their joint distribution P(A,C), possibly via some mechanical model, and then again calculate the sensitivity and specificity of B for detecting "true" (A*=1, C*=1), marginalized over the measurement error.

This is something you could do in the generated quantities block. At each iteration, take the model-predicted latent "true" outcomes A* and C* to be data, and produce a draw from the conditional posteriors for sensitivity P(sens | A*, B, C*) and specificity P(spec | A*, B, C*), which you can define analytically if you assume a beta prior for each. Note that these draws for sensitivity and specificity will not be draws from the joint distribution P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*).

To sample from the joint distribution P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*), you would have to do some mixture magic in the model block, allowing for all potential discrete states of A* and C*.

Hope this helps. I may have misunderstood what you want to do. If so, please provide more detail on the context.

Luc

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
parts:
About sampling from the joint distribution P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*), I was just thinking that in this particular problem:

P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*) == P(sens | A*, B, C*) . P(spec | A*, B, C*)

This is because the number of observations with (A*=1,C*=1) only determines the posterior uncertainty in sensitivity; posterior uncertainty in specificity is determined by the number of observations with !(A*=1,C*=1).

messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: Re: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
parts:
Hi Bob, Andrew & Luc - 

Thanks for the replies; lots to chew over, and will come back with an update when I take a swing at these ideas!

Sorry for being vague in the original. The exposure, "A", is an episode of household exposure to tuberculosis that has been documented. The test, "B", is a tuberculin skin test (TST), which is very rough, left-censored measure of tuberculosis infection, and the outcome, "C" is developing TB disease during the year after exposure. A positive TST strongly suggests that an individual was infected with TB at some time before testing positive, but gives no indication of when. Individuals testing positive for TB using the TST are more likely than TST-negative folks to develop disease, but still not terribly likely to do so (< 1%). The caveat is that individuals who might have been TST-negative but for some known source of intensive exposure (either b/c they have relatively few exposure risks or are too young to have had a lot of community exposure) should be much more likely to develop disease. So the idea is to get an estimate of how much of the overall risk of developing TB disease is attributable to that household exposure, both via exposure causing a change in TST status, i.e. the A -> B -> C pathway, or exposure not causing a change in TST status (what I called the A->C pathways), either because it doesn't stimulate a response (i.e. the person remains TST-negative) or they were already TST positive before the exposure.

Andrew - in terms of modeling the joint outcome, are you suggesting something like a multinomial logit for each B/C combination, or just modeling P(C|B)*P(B)? 

Thanks!

-Jon
